t: Why Consistency Is Everything The First Two Weeks Of The School Year
q: The first two weeks of the school year is the honeymoon period. Students are eager and wanting to please.
You’ve sent a message to the entire class that you don’t really mean what you say and have now put yourself in position to judge subjectively when and whether a student deserves a consequence.
You see, minor, seemingly harmless misbehavior in the beginning always leads to major disruptions once the honeymoon period ends.
So many students have had teachers in the past who post rules and consequences, but only kinda-sorta follow them. And they assume you’ll be like all the rest.
First, you must know precisely what does and doesn’t constitute breaking your rules . Because if you’re unsure, then you can’t possibly be consistent.
Visualize yourself recognizing misbehavior when it happens, calmly enforcing your plan like a referee , and then moving on as if nothing happened.
x: The first two weeks of school are described as a 'honeymoon period' where small exceptions to rules can quietly undermine consistency for the rest of the year.
Concrete examples show how minor rule-breaking that seems harmless in the moment signals to students that the teacher doesn't fully mean what they say.

He argues students test boundaries in small ways early on specifically to learn whether a teacher is a person of their word, since many past teachers have posted rules they didn't consistently enforce.
A key recommendation is knowing precisely, in advance, what does and doesn't constitute breaking each classroom rule.
A daily few-minute visualization ritual before school is proposed to mentally commit to enforcing the plan exactly as written, like a referee.

t: 3 Things You Must Do On The First Day Of School https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/08/18/3-things-you-must-do-on-the-first-day-of-school/
q: The tendency is to rush. To try and cover every policy and procedure. To cram it all in on the first day of school for fear that if you don’t, then your students will develop bad habits.
But the truth is, you only really need to focus on three things.
It’s best to start by explaining why you have a classroom management plan to begin with and how it protects their right to learn and enjoy school.
That first routine you teach, however, is especially important because it provides a model for how all other routines should be performed.
You see, on the first day of school your students are most open and ready to learn. They’re eager to turn over a new leaf and you must take advantage of it.

So double-down on what matters most. Teach boldly and courageously. Leave your students at the end of the first day excited, happily shaken, and wholly different than when they walked through your door.
x: These three elements are framed as establishing classroom culture more effectively than attempting to cover every policy and procedure on the first day.
Rather than rushing through every policy, Linsin argues teachers should focus on three things on day one: one overview, one routine, one lesson.
The classroom management plan overview (20-30 minutes) should explain its purpose, read the plan aloud, and 'visualize' a misbehaving student's path through consequences.
The first routine taught sets the model and standard for how all subsequent routines will be learned, with modeling intensity varying by grade band.
For the lesson, he urges teachers to choose one clear, challenging objective and teach it with full passion and performance, since students are most open to influence on day one.
For the day's lesson, teachers should choose one clear, worthwhile objective and teach it with full passion since students are most receptive on day one.

t: Why You Should Be Openly Friendly On The First Day Of School https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/08/11/be-openly-friendly-on-the-first-day-of-school/
q: Surprisingly, it’s still common advice: Never smile the first month or two of the school year.
The truth is, your students will only view you as a pushover if you fail to do what you say you’re going to do.
A warm and welcoming manner draws students to you. It causes them to want to be around you and get to know you better, which in turn builds fast, easy, and natural rapport .
Because it puts students at ease, a calm and friendly nature virtually eliminates excitability , which is one of the biggest causes of misbehavior—especially among your most challenging students.
When students first realize that they like their new teacher, their appreciation creates a strong desire to return your kindness. It makes them want to listen to you, behave for you, and please you.
My number one goal on that first day isn’t that my students can perform every routine perfectly. It’s that they love coming to my classroom.
x: Linsin refutes the common advice to withhold smiling for the first weeks of school, arguing pushover status comes from failing to follow through, not from kindness.

t: Should You Enforce A Consequence For Inattentiveness? tentiveness/
q: Should you or shouldn’t you enforce a consequence when you notice a student daydreaming? Or staring off into space. Or otherwise not paying attention.
Children learn in different ways, and just because they’re not looking at you doesn’t necessarily mean that they’re not listening.

A classroom management plan is designed to address misbehavior only. When you extend it beyond it’s intended job, you anger and confuse your students and make it difficult to know when to enforce a consequence.

When you notice students yawning, sighing, and looking around the room, it’s a clear sign that they’re bored . They’re giving you feedback that your lesson isn’t hitting its mark or that they need a break.
It’s best to think of it as a failure to follow a direct instruction.
x: Enforcing a consequence for apparent inattentiveness (e.g., daydreaming) is argued to be a mistake, despite seeming to fall under 'Listen and Follow Directions.'
Inattentiveness is called impossible to judge accurately, since a student not looking at the teacher may still be listening.
A classroom management plan should address disruptive misbehavior only, not internal states like boredom or daydreaming.

He gives three reasons: inattentiveness is impossible to judge accurately since a student not looking at the teacher may still be listening; a classroom management plan should address only genuinely disruptive…
The rule 'Listen and Follow Directions' is clarified to mean failure to follow a specific, already-taught instruction—an observable, enforceable behavior rather than a judgment of attention.
